entries.location: Chapter 6 Vector Calculus: Section 6.8 The Divergence Theorem
entries.detail:
You corrected question 385 in Chapter 6.8 from 1/3 \pi to 4/3 \pi.   This is because ( I assume ) you decided that the surface S of the hemisphere includes the bottom disk in the z=0 plane.    This is an assumption that needs to be stated, otherwise the question is poorly defined.    If S includes the bottom disk then the correction is valid and the solution is 4/3 \pi.  If S does not include the bottom disk ( as is typically assumed in such questions) then you need to subtract the surface integral over the bottom disk, which is \pi,  and hence the original solution was correct  and should revert back to 1/3 \pi.
In either case it makes sense to explicitly state in the question if the bottom disk is part  of S or not!


There is no reason to have the question hinge on how one interprets S.

entries.detail:
From the statement of the theorem, "Let F be a vector field in two or three dimensions such that the component functions of F have continuous second-order mixed-partial derivatives on the domain of F."  

The proof of the theorem uses that the potential function for F has continuous mixed derivatives when it uses Clairaut's theorem (theorem 4.5 in section 4.3).  And so what's needed is that the first derivatives of the components of F are continuous, not the second derivatives.  To be really refined it only requires that certain first derivatives of the components of F a are continuous but that's really going into the weeds.

TLDR: I think theorem 6.2 should refer to continuous first derivatives not continuous second-order mixed partials.

This correction will then confirm your conclusion in the later sentence "To compute the flow rate of the fluid in Example 6.68, we simply remove the density constant, which gives a flow rate of  90π m^3/sec.".  

(3) This final item is not a correction, but just a suggestion. In the discussion beginning with "In Example 6.70, we computed the mass flux, which is the rate of mass flow per unit area. If we want to find the flow rate (measured in volume per time) instead, we can use flux integral  ∫∫Sv∙NdS, which leaves out the density." Since the term "flow rate" is thrown around a lot in this section, I think referring to this new integral (without density) as "volumetric flow rate" would make things clearer. This is a standard term for this quantity.
